title: CLAT — English Language | Sentence Correction
description: Subject-wise test on Sentence Correction (English Language) for CLAT. 20Q.
subject: clat-english

questions.question: Neither the lawyers nor the client were happy with the verdict.

options.text: Neither the lawyers nor the client was happy with the verdict.
options.explanation: Correct application of subject-verb agreement rule.

options.text: Neither the lawyers nor the client were happy by the verdict.
options.explanation: Incorrect preposition and subject-verb agreement.

options.text: Neither the lawyers nor the client are happy with the verdict.
options.explanation: Incorrect subject-verb agreement.

options.text: The lawyers and the client were neither happy with the verdict.
options.explanation: Changes the meaning and is grammatically incorrect.

questions.explanation: When "neither... nor" connects two subjects, the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. In this case, "client" is singular, so the verb should be "was" (singular) instead of "were" (plural).
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: The committee decided to postpone their meeting until next month due to unforeseen circumstances.

options.text: The committee decided to postpone their meeting until next month due to unforeseen circumstances.
options.explanation: Incorrect pronoun for a collective noun.

options.text: The committee decided to postpone its meeting until next month due to unforeseen circumstances.
options.explanation: Correct use of singular pronoun for a collective noun.

options.text: The committee decided to postpone its meeting until next month because of unforeseen circumstances.
options.explanation: While grammatically correct, the preposition change is not necessary.

options.text: The committee decided to postpone their meeting until next month because of unforeseen circumstances.
options.explanation: Incorrect pronoun for a collective noun.

questions.explanation: "Committee" is a collective noun. When acting as a single, cohesive unit (as it is here, making a single decision), it takes a singular pronoun ("its") rather than a plural one ("their").
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: To succeed in this competitive field, one must be dedicated, possess strong analytical skills, and able to communicate effectively.

options.text: To succeed in this competitive field, one must be dedicated, possess strong analytical skills, and be able to communicate effectively.
options.explanation: Maintains parallel structure with infinitive phrases.

options.text: To succeed in this competitive field, one must be dedicated, possessing strong analytical skills, and able to communicate effectively.
options.explanation: Lacks parallel structure due to the participle "possessing".

options.text: To succeed in this competitive field, one must be dedicated, possess strong analytical skills, and communicates effectively.
options.explanation: Incorrect verb tense and lack of parallel structure.

options.text: To succeed in this competitive field, one must be dedicated, possess strong analytical skills, and also effectively communicate.
options.explanation: Changes the sentence structure and meaning.

questions.explanation: This sentence requires parallel structure for the list of qualities following "one must." The items in the list should be grammatically consistent.
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: Having finished their extensive research, the new policy was presented by the team.

options.text: Having finished their extensive research, the new policy was presented by the team.
options.explanation: Dangling modifier incorrectly modifies "the new policy".

options.text: Having finished their extensive research, the team presented the new policy.
options.explanation: Correctly places the subject "the team" after the introductory phrase.

options.text: The new policy was presented by the team, having finished their extensive research.
options.explanation: Changes the sentence structure but still contains a dangling modifier.

options.text: When their extensive research was finished, the new policy was presented by the team.
options.explanation: Changes the sentence structure and meaning, and does not address the dangling modifier issue.

questions.explanation: The original sentence contains a dangling modifier. The introductory phrase describes the agent performing the action, which must be the subject immediately following the comma.
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: The recent economic downturn, which has affected several industries, have led to significant job losses across the country.

options.text: The recent economic downturn, which has affected several industries, have led to significant job losses across the country.
options.explanation: Incorrect subject-verb agreement.

options.text: The recent economic downturn, which has affected several industries, has led to significant job losses across the country.
options.explanation: Correct subject-verb agreement.

options.text: The recent economic downturn, affecting several industries, have led to significant job losses across the country.
options.explanation: Incorrect subject-verb agreement and sentence structure.

options.text: The recent economic downturn, which had affected several industries, has led to significant job losses across the country.
options.explanation: Changes the verb tense unnecessarily.

questions.explanation: The main subject of the sentence is "The recent economic downturn" (singular). The verb for this subject should also be singular.
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: Despite her initial apprehension, she quickly adapted _______ the demands of her new role.

options.text: to
options.explanation: Correct preposition to use with "adapt".

options.text: with
options.explanation: Incorrect preposition to use with "adapt" in this context.

options.text: for
options.explanation: Incorrect preposition to use with "adapt" in this context.

options.text: into
options.explanation: Incorrect preposition to use with "adapt" in this context.

questions.explanation: The verb "adapt" typically takes the preposition "to" when referring to adjusting oneself or something to a new situation or condition.
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: The report concluded that the company's financial performance was more worse than initially projected.

options.text: more worse
options.explanation: Double comparative error.

options.text: much worse
options.explanation: Correct intensification of the comparative form.

options.text: more bad
options.explanation: Incorrect comparative form.

options.text: worst
options.explanation: Superlative form used incorrectly in this context.

questions.explanation: "Worse" is already the comparative form of "bad." Using "more" before "worse" creates a double comparative, which is grammatically incorrect.
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: The manager made it clear that he would not tolerate employees to be late for meetings.

options.text: The manager made it clear that he would not tolerate employees to be late for meetings.
options.explanation: Incorrect use of infinitive after "tolerate".

options.text: The manager made it clear that he would not tolerate employees being late for meetings.
options.explanation: Correct use of gerund after "tolerate".

options.text: The manager made it clear that he would not tolerate employees who were late for meetings.
options.explanation: Changes the meaning to focus on the employees themselves.

options.text: The manager made it clear that he would not tolerate that employees are late for meetings.
options.explanation: Grammatically awkward and incorrect.

questions.explanation: The verb "tolerate" is generally followed by a gerund or a noun phrase.
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: Unlike the previous generation, today's youth is more aware of environmental issues and more proactive in addressing them.

options.text: Unlike the previous generation, today's youth is more aware of environmental issues and more proactive in addressing them.
options.explanation: Incorrect subject-verb agreement.

options.text: Unlike the previous generation, today's youth are more aware of environmental issues and more proactive in addressing them.
options.explanation: Correct subject-verb agreement and logical comparison.

options.text: Different from the previous generation, today's youth is more aware of environmental issues and more proactive in addressing them.
options.explanation: Incorrect subject-verb agreement and preposition.

options.text: Today's youth, unlike the previous generation, is more aware of environmental issues and more proactive in addressing them.
options.explanation: Incorrect subject-verb agreement.

questions.explanation: This question tests both subject-verb agreement and logical comparison.
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: Which of the following sentences uses the correct subject-verb agreement for the collective noun 'youth' when referring to the individual members being aware and proactive?

options.text: Youth is aware and proactive.
options.explanation: Incorrect use of 'is' with 'youth' when referring to individual members.

options.text: Youth are aware and proactive.
options.explanation: Correct use of 'are' with 'youth' when referring to individual members.

options.text: Youth is different from other groups in being aware and proactive.
options.explanation: Incorrect comparison and use of 'is' with 'youth'.

options.text: Youth is unlike other groups in being aware and proactive.
options.explanation: Incorrect use of 'is' with 'youth' when referring to individual members.

questions.explanation: The collective noun 'youth' can be treated as singular or plural depending on the context. When referring to the individual members being aware and proactive, it requires a plural verb.
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: Select the sentence that is grammatically correct and conveys the intended meaning most clearly.

options.text: The new policy is designed not only to improve efficiency but also promoting employee satisfaction.
options.explanation: Breaks parallelism by using a gerund ('promoting') after 'but also'.

options.text: The new policy is designed not only to improve efficiency but also to promote employee satisfaction.
options.explanation: Correctly maintains parallelism by using an infinitive phrase ('to promote employee satisfaction') after 'but also'.

options.text: The new policy is designed not only for improving efficiency but also for promoting employee satisfaction.
options.explanation: Changes the preposition and structure, which is less direct and less parallel to the original intention.

options.text: The new policy is designed not only to improve efficiency, but also promoting employee satisfaction.
options.explanation: Breaks parallelism by using a gerund ('promoting') after 'but also'.

questions.explanation: The sentence requires parallel structure with the correlative conjunction 'not only... but also'. The phrase following 'not only' must be grammatically parallel to the phrase following 'but also'.
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: Identify the grammatically correct sentence:

options.text: Each of the students have been asked to submit their project by Friday.
options.explanation: The subject 'Each' is singular, but the verb 'have' is plural.

options.text: Each of the students has been asked to submit their project by Friday.
options.explanation: The pronoun 'their' is plural, but it should be singular ('his or her' or 'his/her') to maintain formal agreement.

options.text: Each of the students has been asked to submit his or her project by Friday.
options.explanation: The subject 'Each' is singular, and the verb 'has been asked' is singular. The pronoun 'his or her' is also singular, maintaining formal agreement.

options.text: Each of the students have been asked to submit his or her project by Friday.
options.explanation: The subject 'Each' is singular, but the verb 'have' is plural.

questions.explanation: The subject 'Each' is singular, so the verb must be singular ('has been asked'). Additionally, the pronoun referring back to 'Each' should also be singular ('his or her' or 'his/her'), maintaining formal agreement.
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: Choose the option that best corrects the underlined part of the sentence:

options.text: along with several controversial amendments, are expected to be implemented next month.
options.explanation: The verb 'are' is plural, but it should be singular ('is') to agree with the singular subject 'policy'.

options.text: along with several controversial amendments, is expected to be implemented next month.
options.explanation: The verb 'is' is singular, agreeing with the singular subject 'policy'.

options.text: along with several controversial amendments, expects to be implemented next month.
options.explanation: The verb 'expects' is incorrect, as it does not agree with the singular subject 'policy' in the passive voice.

options.text: along with several controversial amendments, were expected to be implemented next month.
options.explanation: The verb 'were' is plural, but it should be singular ('is') to agree with the singular subject 'policy'.

questions.explanation: In this sentence, 'The new policy' is the singular subject. Phrases like 'along with,' 'as well as,' 'in addition to,' etc., are not part of the subject and do not affect the verb's number. Therefore, the singular verb 'is expected' is required to agree with the singular subject 'policy.'
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: Select the option that corrects the error in parallelism in the sentence:

options.text: hiking in the mountains, visiting ancient ruins, and relaxing by the lake.
options.explanation: All items in the list are in the same grammatical form (gerunds), maintaining parallelism.

options.text: hiking in the mountains, to visit ancient ruins, and relaxing by the lake.
options.explanation: The items in the list are not in the same grammatical form, as 'hiking' and 'relaxing' are gerunds, but 'to visit' is an infinitive.

options.text: to hike in the mountains, visiting ancient ruins, and relaxing by the lake.
options.explanation: The items in the list are not in the same grammatical form, as 'visiting' and 'relaxing' are gerunds, but 'to hike' is an infinitive.

options.text: hiking in the mountains, visiting ancient ruins, and to relax at the lake.
options.explanation: The items in the list are not in the same grammatical form, as 'hiking' and 'visiting' are gerunds, but 'to relax' is an infinitive.

questions.explanation: For parallelism, all items in a list or series should have the same grammatical form. In the original sentence, 'hiking' (gerund) and 'visiting' (gerund) are followed by 'to relax' (infinitive). To maintain parallelism, 'to relax' must be changed to 'relaxing' (gerund).
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: Identify the sentence that contains a misplaced modifier:

options.text: Covered in dust, the old book lay forgotten on the shelf.
options.explanation: The modifier 'Covered in dust' is correctly placed, as it clearly describes 'the old book'.

options.text: The detective interviewed the witness, who had seen the crime, in his office.
options.explanation: There is no misplaced modifier in this sentence.

options.text: He bought a car from a dealer with leather seats.
options.explanation: The phrase 'with leather seats' is a misplaced modifier, as it grammatically modifies 'dealer' instead of 'car'.

options.text: Running quickly, the athlete crossed the finish line.
options.explanation: The modifier 'Running quickly' is correctly placed, as it clearly describes 'the athlete'.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'with leather seats' is a misplaced modifier. Grammatically, it appears to modify 'dealer,' suggesting the dealer has leather seats. Logically, it should modify 'car.' The sentence should be rephrased as 'He bought a car with leather seats from a dealer.'
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: Choose the best way to complete the sentence:

options.text: was
options.explanation: The verb 'was' is in the indicative mood, not the subjunctive mood required for hypothetical conditions.

options.text: am
options.explanation: The verb 'am' is in the present tense and indicative mood, not suitable for a hypothetical past condition.

options.text: were
options.explanation: The verb 'were' is in the subjunctive mood, which is correct for expressing a hypothetical or contrary-to-fact condition.

options.text: have been
options.explanation: The verb 'have been' is in the present perfect tense and indicative mood, not suitable for a hypothetical past condition.

questions.explanation: This sentence expresses a hypothetical or contrary-to-fact condition, which requires the use of the subjunctive mood. In such constructions, 'were' is used for all subjects (I, he, she, it, we, they) in the 'if' clause, regardless of whether the subject is singular or plural.
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is the most concise and grammatically correct?

options.text: Despite the fact that he was feeling ill, he still managed to arrive at the meeting on time.
options.explanation: The phrase 'Despite the fact that' is wordy and can be replaced with 'Although' for conciseness.

options.text: Although he was feeling ill, he still managed to arrive at the meeting on time.
options.explanation: The conjunction 'Although' is concise and correctly conveys the concessive relationship.

options.text: In spite of the fact that he was feeling ill, he still managed to arrive at the meeting on time.
options.explanation: The phrase 'In spite of the fact that' is wordy and can be replaced with 'Although' for conciseness.

options.text: Due to the fact that he was feeling ill, he still managed to arrive at the meeting on time.
options.explanation: The phrase 'Due to the fact that' implies cause and effect, not concession, and is wordy.

questions.explanation: Options A and C use the wordy phrases 'Despite the fact that' and 'In spite of the fact that,' which can be replaced by the more concise conjunction 'Although' or 'Despite/In spite of his illness.' Option D uses 'Due to the fact that,' which implies cause and effect, not concession. 'Although' directly conveys the concessive relationship concisely.
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: Identify the grammatically correct sentence:

options.text: Neither the manager nor the employees is happy with the new policy changes.
options.explanation: The verb 'is' is singular, but it should be plural ('are') because 'employees' is the subject closer to the verb.

options.text: Neither the manager nor the employees are happy with the new policy changes.
options.explanation: The verb 'are' is plural, agreeing with 'employees,' the subject closer to the verb.

options.text: Neither the manager nor the employees has been happy with the new policy changes.
options.explanation: The verb 'has been' is singular, but it should be plural ('have been') because 'employees' is the subject closer to the verb.

options.text: Neither the manager nor the employees have been happy with the new policy changes.
options.explanation: Although the verb 'have been' is plural, the sentence is in the present perfect tense, which is not the focus of the question.

questions.explanation: When 'neither...nor' connects two subjects, the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. In this case, 'employees' (plural) is closer to the verb, so the plural verb 'are' is correct.
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: Choose the option that best corrects the underlined portion of the sentence:

options.text: superior than
options.explanation: The preposition 'than' is incorrect; 'to' should be used after 'superior'.

options.text: superior to
options.explanation: The preposition 'to' is correct after 'superior' in comparative constructions.

options.text: more superior than
options.explanation: The phrase 'more superior' is redundant and incorrect, and 'than' is the wrong preposition to use with 'superior'.

options.text: superior as
options.explanation: The preposition 'as' is not the correct preposition to use after 'superior' in comparative constructions.

questions.explanation: The adjective 'superior' is always followed by the preposition 'to,' not 'than,' when making a comparison. It is an absolute comparative adjective, similar to 'inferior,' 'senior,' 'junior,' 'prior,' etc.
questions.subject: clat-english

questions.question: Select the grammatically correct sentence:

options.text: No sooner had the bell rung, when the students rushed out of the classroom.
options.explanation: The conjunction 'when' is incorrect; 'than' should be used after 'No sooner'.

options.text: No sooner had the bell rung, than the students rushed out of the classroom.
options.explanation: The conjunction 'than' is correct after 'No sooner', and the inversion 'had the bell rung' is correct.

options.text: No sooner did the bell ring, when the students rushed out of the classroom.
options.explanation: The conjunction 'when' is incorrect; 'than' should be used after 'No sooner'. Also, 'did the bell ring' is not the correct form for the past perfect inversion required by 'No sooner'.

options.text: No sooner did the bell ring, than the students rushed out of the classroom.
options.explanation: Although 'than' is correct, 'did the bell ring' is not the correct form for the past perfect inversion; 'had the bell rung' is needed for the correct past perfect construction.

questions.explanation: The correlative conjunction 'No sooner' must be followed by 'than.' Also, when 'No sooner' begins a sentence, it requires inversion (auxiliary verb before the subject), so 'had the bell rung' is correct. Option D uses 'did the bell ring' which is also correct for inversion, but the past participle 'rung' (from 'to ring') is needed after 'had'. So, 'No sooner had the bell rung' is the correct past perfect construction for the inverted clause.
questions.subject: clat-english
